source.title_on_document: The Pedagogical Impact of ChatGPT on High-school Student’s Creative Writing Skills: An Exploration of Generative AI Assisted Writing Tools

paper_design_summary: The paper reports random allocation of 84 eleventh-grade students at Angsilapittayakom School in Thailand to ChatGPT-integrated or conventional classroom writing lessons, despite calling the design quasi-experimental (PDF pp. 4-5, printed pp. 20-21). Both groups received 20 hours of instruction and wrote unassisted narratives before and after instruction, scored by the researcher and two native speakers (PDF pp. 5-10, printed pp. 21-26). Only the total creative-writing rubric score has comparative results; the posttest analysis sample sizes are not stated (PDF pp. 11-12, printed pp. 27-28, Tables 3-4).

studies.label: ChatGPT-integrated creative-writing lessons and unassisted writing posttest

assignment.what_was_assigned: Individual students were allocated to Group A (ChatGPT-integrated lessons) or Group B (conventional lessons). Explicit random group-allocation statements support field_rct despite the author's quasi-experimental label. The allocation algorithm and concealment are not detailed. Assignment is between groups, with repeated pretest and posttest assessment within each group (PDF pp. 4-5, printed pp. 20-21; classroom setting in PDF pp. 5-6).
assignment.quote: Employing a simple random sampling method, these students were then allocated into two distinct groups, namely Group A (Experimental Group) and Group B (Controlled Group), each comprising 42 students.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 21), Population and Samples; corroborating random group-allocation statement and quasi-experimental label in PDF p. 4 (printed p. 20), Methodology; classroom lesson setting in PDF pp. 5-6 (printed pp. 21-22), Research Instruments.

arms.name: Group A (Experimental Group)
arms.description: Communicative Language Teaching integrated with ChatGPT for outlining, drafting, revisions, and feedback; 10 lesson plans for 20 hours (PDF pp. 5-6, printed pp. 21-22, Research Instruments, item 1). Allocation N = 42 is stated in Population and Samples (PDF p. 5); analyzed N = 42 is explicitly printed for the pretest in Table 2 (PDF p. 10). The posttest N is not separately printed in Tables 3-4.

arms.name: Group B (Controlled Group)
arms.description: Conventional Communicative Language Teaching without AI-assisted writing tools, with the same teaching stages and 10 lesson plans for 20 hours (PDF p. 6, printed p. 22, Research Instruments, item 2). Allocation N = 42 is stated in Population and Samples (PDF p. 5); analyzed N = 42 is explicitly printed for the pretest in Table 2 (PDF p. 10). The posttest N is not separately printed in Table 4.

participants.exclusions: No exclusions or attrition are stated. The document reports 84 sampled/allocated students and Table 2 explicitly gives pretest N = 42 per arm. Tables 3-4 omit posttest analysis Ns and the number of complete pairs. Final analyzed counts are therefore null; pretest counts are preserved here without being substituted for the posttest sample. No intention-to-treat analysis is claimed (PDF p. 5, printed p. 21, Population and Samples; PDF pp. 10-12, printed pp. 26-28, Tables 2-4).
participants.who: Eleventh-grade students from Angsilapittayakom School, within the Chonburi-Rayong Secondary Educational Service Area, in the second semester of the 2023 academic year (PDF p. 5, printed p. 21, Population and Samples).
participants.quote: A meticulous multi-stage sampling method was employed to randomly select 84 eleventh- grade students from Angsilapittayakom School as the study’s samples.
participants.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 21), Population and Samples, gives 84 sampled/allocated students and 42 per group; PDF p. 10 (printed p. 26), Table 2, gives pretest N = 42 per group; PDF pp. 11-12 (printed pp. 27-28), Tables 3-4, omit final analyzed Ns. Thai context: PDF p. 1 (printed p. 17), Abstract.

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT, paid version; specific language model and model version not stated (PDF p. 6, printed p. 22, Research Instruments).
ai_tool.how_used: Students were granted access to ChatGPT during their lessons to generate outlines, draft, refine ideas, revise content, and obtain feedback. Introductory training covered the interface, generating prompts, interpreting suggestions, and incorporating feedback. This is coded as open_chat because students directly used the tool, with both ideation and refinement functions (PDF pp. 5-6, printed pp. 21-22, Research Instruments, item 1). ChatGPT was unavailable during the scored pretest and posttest because devices and internet resources were prohibited (PDF pp. 7, 9-10, printed pp. 23, 25-26).

task.description: Write an English narrative from a researcher-provided prompt, with a different prompt at posttest. Examples concerned an abandoned house, a deserted island, a journal entry, and dialogue in a mysterious situation. Resulting narratives typically ranged from 300 to 500 words; this is a descriptive range, not a stated word-limit requirement (PDF pp. 7-8, printed pp. 23-24, Creative Writing Skills Assessment; PDF p. 10, printed p. 26, Post-Learning Assessment).
task.duration: 10 lesson plans covering 20 hours in each group; 50 minutes for each pretest and posttest narrative. The calendar span of instruction and any interval in days after the last lesson are not stated (PDF pp. 5-7, 9-10, printed pp. 21-23, 25-26).

outcomes.name: Creative writing skills total score at the unassisted posttest
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Total score of 25 points across five dimensions, each worth 5 points: Creativity, Development, Voice, Literary Devices, and Literary Conventions (PDF pp. 8-9, printed pp. 24-25, Table 1; PDF pp. 11-12, printed pp. 27-28, Tables 3-4). The researcher and two native speakers rated each narrative. Panel coded as expert_raters under the codebook's instructor/professional category: the researcher is the school's Head of Research for Educational Development Subdivision and assigned classroom writing tasks (PDF p. 1, printed p. 17, author affiliation; PDF p. 6, printed p. 22, Research Instruments, item 2). The two native speakers' professional qualifications are not stated; they are not assumed to be experts. Rater blinding and the method of combining ratings are not stated. The paper also describes three experts validating the rubric but does not establish whether these were different people from the output raters (PDF p. 7, printed p. 23, Creative Writing Skills Assessment). The total combines creativity and writing-quality criteria. It is the outcome for both stated research objectives, supporting paper_primary (PDF p. 4, printed p. 20, Research Objectives). Only the total has comparative results; the five components below have no separate estimates (PDF pp. 11-12, Tables 3-4). The posttest prohibited electronic devices and internet resources and therefore answers after_ai (PDF p. 10, printed p. 26, Data Collection, step 4).
outcomes.delay: Posttest upon completion of the teaching sessions; no elapsed interval in days or later retention assessment is stated (PDF p. 10, printed p. 26, Data Collection, step 4).

contrasts.reported: Posttest total score (25 points): Group A M = 22.72, S.D. = 5.72; Group B M = 19.82, S.D. = 7.42; t = 14.46; Sig. = 0.00*. The footnote states statistical significance at a 0.01 level. Values are retained as printed. Table 4 does not give posttest N, degrees of freedom, standard errors, confidence intervals, or standardized effects. Table 2 gives pretest N = 42 per arm, which is not confirmation of posttest N. The arm_means_sds_ns flag is omitted because the relevant analysis Ns are unknown, although means and SDs are printed.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 12 (printed p. 28), Table 4 and Findings; independent-samples method in PDF p. 11 (printed p. 27), Data Analysis, item 3; baseline-only Ns in PDF p. 10 (printed p. 26), Table 2.

contrasts.reported: Group A total score (25 points): before the integration of Generative AI tools M = 11.46, S.D. = 7.12; after the integration of Generative AI tools M = 22.72, S.D. = 5.72; paired-samples t = 17.91; Sig. = 0.00*. The footnote states statistical significance at a 0.01 level. Table 3 does not give the number of complete pairs, degrees of freedom, paired-difference SD, standard errors, confidence intervals, or standardized effects. Table 2 gives pretest N = 42 for Group A, which is not confirmation of complete-pair N. This is a within-group change in the same study, not a separate randomized contrast. The arm_means_sds_ns flag is omitted because the complete-pair N is unknown.

eligibility.reason: Random allocation of individual students to ChatGPT-integrated versus conventional classroom lessons is explicit, supporting field_rct despite the quasi-experimental label (PDF pp. 4-5, printed pp. 20-21, Methodology and Population and Samples). The paper reports 84 students randomized, 42 per arm, and Table 2 reports pretest analysis N = 42 per arm. Tables 3-4 and the posttest procedure provide no posttest analysis Ns, complete-pair N, or retention accounting; the allocation and baseline counts do not confirm at least 50 people analyzed on the post-intervention outcome. Criterion 2 and core eligibility remain unclear (PDF p. 5 and pp. 10-12, printed pp. 21 and 26-28, Population and Samples, Post-Learning Assessment, and Tables 2-4). The researcher and two native speakers scored student-written narratives on a rubric including creativity and originality, so criterion 3 is met; the panel includes an education professional and is coded expert_raters, with the other raters' professional qualifications unreported (PDF p. 1, affiliation; PDF pp. 6-9, printed pp. 22-25, Research Instruments and Table 1). Electronic devices and internet resources were prohibited during the posttest, establishing after_ai (PDF p. 10, printed p. 26, Post-Learning Assessment).

one_line_finding: Unassisted writing scored 22.72 (SD 5.72) after ChatGPT lessons versus 19.82 (SD 7.42) after conventional lessons on a 25-point scale (PDF p. 12, Table 4; printed t = 14.46, Sig. = 0.00*).
open_questions: How many students contributed to each posttest and how many complete pairs entered Table 3? Allocation and pretest counts are explicit, but Tables 3-4 omit analysis Ns and no attrition account is given; this prevents confirming the analyzed-sample eligibility threshold (PDF pp. 5 and 10-12, printed pp. 21 and 26-28).

Were the rubric-validation experts and output raters different people, and what were the two native speakers' professional qualifications? The researcher's education-professional and classroom role is documented, but the panels' identities and overlap, the other raters' qualifications, the score-aggregation rule, and rater blinding are unreported (PDF p. 1, printed p. 17, affiliation; PDF pp. 6-7, printed pp. 22-23, Research Instruments).

How was random group allocation implemented? Explicit random-allocation wording supports the design classification, but the paper also calls the design quasi-experimental and does not describe the allocation algorithm or concealment (PDF pp. 4-5, printed pp. 20-21).

Verify the printed test statistics, particularly Table 4's t = 14.46 and Sig. = 0.00*, against the underlying data before quantitative synthesis; retain the printed means, SDs, and test statistics without calculating replacements (PDF pp. 11-12, printed pp. 27-28, Tables 3-4).
notes: Reconciled on 2026-10-09 from both parseable raw forms. Read the full 411-line markdown conversion in chunks and extracted text from all 18 PDF pages, including references; no appendix is appended and no supplement is mentioned. Every retained numeric fact was checked against its PDF page, with table recovery used for Tables 1-4. Locators identify physical PDF pages and, where useful, printed journal pages. Baseline Table 2 prints Group A N = 42, M = 11.46, S.D. = 7.12; Group B N = 42, M = 12.86, S.D. = 8.23; t = 1.04; Sig. = 0.35. The footnote states no statistical significance at a 0.01 level (PDF p. 10, printed p. 26). This is baseline balance information, not an AI-effect estimate. The outcome inventory contains one total and five explicitly scored rubric components; only the total has comparative results, so the components are not five additional effect estimates. Figures 1-2 describe teaching procedures. Lesson-plan quality and rubric-validation/reliability statistics are instrument checks, not participant-output outcomes. No diversity or delayed-retention outcome, shared participant sample, preregistration, data URL, or code URL is reported. No effect sizes or replacement test statistics were computed. Sig. = 0.00* is kept as printed, without interpreting it as an exact zero probability. Both screeners used baseline Ns for the analyzed-count fields and the arm_means_sds_ns flags; the reconciled form uses null for posttest analyzed Ns and omits that flag, while preserving all printed means and SDs. The sample-size criterion and core decision are consequently unclear. Reconciliation differences count substantive factual additions and the rater-panel identity claim; equivalent arm names, phrasing, locator formatting, fuller front-matter dates, and empty synthesis defaults are not substantive differences. Repeated claims across outcome descriptions are grouped into one difference. n_unresolved counts one unresolved screener difference plus one unconfirmed agreed fact (posttest analysis N and its dependent eligibility/statistics fields); each underlying issue is counted once. Other reporting limitations remain in open_questions. Finalized on 2026-10-09 after independently reading all 411 markdown lines, including references; no appendix or supplementary-material reference was found. Relevant PDF passages and all retained source numbers were checked with PyMuPDF text extraction; table extraction was also attempted for Tables 1-4. All three outcome-checker problems were corrected: the panel is coded expert_raters because it includes a documented education professional, with the native speakers' qualifications left unspecified, and Voice and Literary Devices are coded usefulness. Assignment and people challenge files contained no problems. Source.supplement already matches the current spec (not_stated, not in this PDF). The study is an original classroom experiment, not a reanalysis; field_rct remains supported by explicit random allocation. Counts remain separated into randomized, baseline analyzed, and unknown posttest analyzed counts; no exclusions or retention counts were invented. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged as the historical reconciliation record, including its previous human_raters coding. The final object records the subsequent decisions; its n_open counts unresolved challenge problems, while open_items separately records remaining reporting questions. Core eligibility remains unclear solely because the posttest analyzed sample size is unconfirmed. No reported statistics were changed and no effect sizes were computed.

challenge_resolution.problem: S1-O1 through S1-O6: measure = human_raters classifies the panel as lay raters despite a documented education-professional scorer.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: Changed measure to expert_raters for all six outcomes. The researcher is the school's Head of Research for Educational Development Subdivision and assigned classroom writing tasks, meeting the codebook's instructor/professional category. Each measure_detail now explains this basis and preserves the unknown professional qualifications of the two native speakers; it does not assert that every scorer was an expert. Rater-panel overlap, aggregation, and blinding remain open. Criterion 3 remains met.
